title: Paying for the empty bottle
bodyMd:
When the coastal region of Ostria introduced a deposit-return scheme in 2022, shoppers began paying a deposit of €0.15 on every plastic bottle and drinks can they bought, refunded in full when the empty container was handed back at any shop that sells drinks. Before the scheme, about 40 per cent of such containers in the region were collected for recycling through kerbside bins. By 2024, 88 per cent were being returned.

The scheme is run by a non-profit operator owned jointly by drinks producers and retailers. Its costs, which include the return machines, the counting centres, transport and a handling fee of €0.03 that it pays a shop for each container the shop accepts, are met from three sources: the sale of the collected material to recyclers, a fee charged to producers for every container they put on the market, and the deposits that are never reclaimed. In 2024, when 500 million containers were sold in Ostria, unclaimed deposits brought the operator €9 million.

This last source is where the design becomes awkward. Unclaimed deposits are, in effect, a reward for the scheme's failures: every container that ends up in a hedge or a landfill leaves its €0.15 with the operator. As return rates climb, that income shrinks, and unless something else makes up the difference the operator must raise the producer fee, which producers pass on to shoppers in the shelf price. Critics add that an operator relying heavily on unclaimed deposits has little reason to make returning containers more convenient, for instance by installing machines in small village shops.

Ostria's planners reply that the concern is overstated. Containers returned through the scheme arrive sorted and clean, and the material sells to recyclers for nearly twice the price per tonne of material from kerbside bins, so higher returns raise the operator's income from recyclers even as they reduce its income from unclaimed deposits. Whether the gain outweighs the loss depends on the price of recycled plastic, which has risen or fallen by more than half within a single year more than once in the past decade. The scheme's finances, in other words, may come to depend less on the habits of Ostria's shoppers than on a commodity market that neither the operator nor the region controls.
accessibilityText: A four-paragraph prose passage about a deposit-return scheme for drinks containers in the coastal region of Ostria. There is no table, figure or mathematical notation. The passage states these figures in words: the scheme began in 2022; the deposit is 0.15 euros per plastic bottle or drinks can, refunded in full when the container is returned; before the scheme about 40 per cent of containers were collected through kerbside bins, and by 2024 88 per cent were being returned; the operator pays a shop a handling fee of 0.03 euros for each container the shop accepts; in 2024, 500 million containers were sold and unclaimed deposits brought the operator 9 million euros; returned material sells for nearly twice the price per tonne of kerbside material; the price of recycled plastic has risen or fallen by more than half within a single year more than once in the past decade.

provenance.notes: Original passage written for this item set about a general real subject, deposit-return schemes for drinks containers, in our own words. The region, the operator and every figure are invented, and the figures are consistent: 12 per cent of 500 million containers is 60 million unclaimed containers, and 60 million times 0.15 euros is 9 million euros. The third paragraph raises a concern and the fourth qualifies it, which the implicit-meaning question uses. Nothing is quoted or paraphrased from any published article or test item.
